10.1002_smll.202501825: In this study, we report high-performance perovksite solar cells (PSCs) with rapid photonic annealing (RPA) of all stacking layers, enabled by ultraviolet (UV) light-emitting diode (LED) sources, to replace lengthy and energy-intensive thermal annealing (TA). The UV-LED annealing technique allows for layer-specific annealing, where the selected light source provides a precise UV wavelength for maximizing the amount of light absorption by the target layer. The disparity in optical absorption between the target layer and the underlying films allows the stack of the underlying films to remain relatively unaffected, making this process ideal for heating sensitive substrates. Along with a systematic investigation into the layer-specific annealing mechanism of RPA, the results demonstrated that this UV-LED-based photonic annealing of all stacking layers (7 s for perovskite absorber) can produce PSCs with the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of over 23%, the highest reported among optically annealed PSCs. Moreover, the RPA device retains over 80% of the initial PCE over 1000 h under continuous 1 sun illumination at 55 °C and 30%-60% relative humidity (RH), while TA control device drops to 50% of its initial efficiency. These findings represent significant strides toward achieving rapid, cost-effective, and scalable manufacturing of commercial perovskite photovoltaics (PV).
10.1007_s42114-026-02136-4: Flexible, metal-free humidity sensors with high sensitivity, linear impedance response, and fast response/recovery times are vital for next-generation wearable electronics and environmental monitoring, whereas poor linearity limits the rapid and precise detection of humidity. Here, we report a metal-free humidity sensor that integrates lithographically patterned two-dimensional (2D) Ti 3 C 2 T x -MXene nanosheets (2DMS) interdigital electrodes (IDEs) with an engineered ultrathin network of 2D anatase TiO 2 nanosheets (2DTS) as the active humidity-responsive layer on a cyclic olefin copolymer (COC) substrate. The solution-processed 2DMS IDEs provide high electrical conductivity, mechanical robustness, and scalable patterning, while the 2DTS film forms a continuous, hydroxyl-rich, chemically robust surface network for reversible water adsorption and rapid proton-mediated transport. The resulting 2DMS@2DTS sensor exhibits highly linear and reversible impedance and capacitance modulation across a broad humidity range (6–86% RH), with low hysteresis, minimal change over 24 h, and a sensitivity of 4.41 × 10 5 Ω/%RH at 1 kHz. COMSOL-assisted finite element method (FEM) simulations reveal humidity-induced dielectric redistribution in the IDE’s electric field, while density functional theory (DFT) calculations demonstrate a reduced activation energy for proton (H⁺) migration under humid conditions. These theoretical insights are in excellent agreement with the experimentally observed fast, repeatable response and recovery characteristics, thereby providing a mechanistic understanding of the device’s high-performance humidity-sensing behavior. Owing to its all-2D-materials architecture and flexible COC substrate, the sensor enables practical applications, including real-time physiological monitoring. This work introduces a smart strategy that couples patterned 2DMS electrodes with engineered 2DTS to achieve scalable, metal-free, and flexible humidity sensors, providing a promising platform for wearable and intelligent sensing systems.
10.1016_j.cej.2025.166888: Lithium cobalt oxide (LiCoO 2 ) accounts for over 70 % of global cobalt consumption, primarily in batteries used in consumer electronics. Its conventional synthesis is energy-intensive and relies on increasingly scarce raw materials. Recycling and regeneration of LiCoO 2 have therefore, become critical. Existing recycling methods often involve high energy consumption, complex processing, and material loss. This work reports a hybrid thermochemical regeneration strategy integrating selective leaching, a glucose-assisted self-sustaining reaction, and brief oxidative annealing to recover high-purity LiCoO 2 from spent batteries. Metal nitrates extracted from spent electrodes react with glucose to form Co, CoO, and Li 2 CO 3 in minutes, followed by complete conversion to phase-pure LiCoO 2 at 850 °C within 10 min. These processes generate localized heat, suppress lithium volatilization, and enable ultrafast regeneration, reducing synthesis time by over 50-fold compared to conventional routes. The regenerated LiCoO 2 exhibits high crystallinity and electrochemical performance comparable to commercial materials at 1C, with ~100 % coulombic efficiency and stable cycling. Technometric analysis shows that the process consumes ~8 MJ/kg of feedstock and emits ~800 g CO 2 /kg, the lowest among existing recycling methods. Furthermore, the process yields more valuable products without the need for resynthesis, with a net economic return of ~$3690 per ton of spent LiCoO 2 batteries. • Glucose-fueled reaction regenerates LiCoO 2 in 10 min at 850 °C. • Cobalt forms via nitrate reduction, then reacts with Li 2 CO 3 to yield LiCoO 2. • Regenerated cathodes match commercial ones in capacity and efficiency. • Scalable regeneration achieved using a standard tube furnace and batch cycling. • Lowest CO 2 output and ~ $3690 profit per ton of recycled battery waste.
10.1016_j.enconman.2026.121254: Proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) face severe durability challenges during cold start-up, especially at sub-freezing temperatures. This study presents a new multi-domain and multi-scale modelling framework to predict PEMFC cold start-up behavior and degradation across different ambient temperatures. The framework couples a detailed system-level electrochemical model with a mechanistic catalyst degradation model that captures platinum dissolution and carbon support corrosion in both space and time. The model is calibrated and validated against experimental data from a Toyota Mirai fuel cell electric vehicle over ambient temperatures ranging from –18°C to 35°C, showing excellent agreement with measured voltage and current profiles. Simulations reveal that at –18°C, ice-induced heterogeneities cause severe local hydrogen starvation and high electrode potentials, leading to a catalyst degradation rate more than 100 times higher than during warmer start-ups. Conversely, at 22°C and 35°C, start-ups are rapid with minimal overall degradation. However, a brief spike in the degradation rate is observed at 22°C due to delayed membrane hydration, and at 35°C due to transient fuel starvation. The integrated model provides unprecedented insight into the spatial distribution of reactions and degradation “hot spots” within the cell, elucidating why colder start-ups lead to accelerated degradation. These insights advance the understanding of PEMFC degradation mechanisms under cold-start conditions and serve as the basis for operational strategies to mitigate such degradation. Finally, the modelling framework provides a virtual testbed for optimizing start-up protocols across climates, ultimately improving fuel cell durability and reliability.
10.1016_j.ijdrr.2026.106226: Modeling human-induced emergencies requires a structured representation of interactions among occupants, hazards, and built environments. While existing simulation approaches provide important insights, behavioral processes, hazard progression, and architectural conditions are often examined separately. This study develops a parameterized agent-based modeling framework that integrates heterogeneous occupant behaviors, hazard dynamics, and environmental configurations within a commercially available crowd-simulation platform to extend its usability within the academic and professional communities. The framework comprises environmental modeling, agent definition, interaction logic, risk evaluation, and simulation execution, enabling systematic configuration of behavioral rules and scenario parameters through customized scripting. An Active Shooter Incident (ASI) in a school building is simulated as a demonstrative case study to illustrate the framework's capability to configure and test emergency scenarios under different behavioral, hazard and environmental assumptions. Using the framework, the study examines the effects of classroom occupancy, door width, and door-locking mechanisms on occupant safety, evaluated using a token-based high-risk metric and factorial statistical analysis. Results indicate that higher occupancy increases exposure risk, timely door locking substantially improves safety outcomes, and the influence of door width is context-dependent. The consistency of these patterns with prior research supports the behavioral plausibility of the modeling approach. Overall, the study contributes a practical and extensible framework for operationalizing human–hazard–environment interactions in similar agent-based simulations and for generating scenario-specific insights to support design and preparedness strategies in human-induced emergency contexts.
10.1021_acs.inorgchem.6c00859: ] (pyalk = 2-(pyridin-2-yl)propan-2-oate) has recently demonstrated remarkable electroselectivity (preferential formation of nitrate or nitrite as a function of the applied potential) and chemoselectivity (water vs ammonia oxidation as a function of pH). However, the mechanistic origin of these selectivities remains unclear. Herein, we provide new insights into the complete electrochemical catalytic cycle of ammonia oxidation (AO) in aqueous media from quantum mechanical calculations. Our results show that the transformation does not proceed through a single oxyl-centered pathway, but through competing oxidation-driven sequences that activate Cu complexes to enable successive N-O bond formation. New mechanistic scenarios are identified in which water participates as a nucleophile, while the ammonia buffer plays a crucial role throughout the catalytic cycle. In addition, ammonia saturation enables participation in the secondary coordination sphere, promoting key intermolecular interactions favorable to N-O bond coupling. Finally, we demonstrate that subsequent electrochemical oxidation steps act as the primary driving forces governing the experimentally observed selectivity. Overall, this work establishes an unprecedented mechanistic framework for copper-mediated ammonia oxidation and provides molecular-level insights into the factors that control selectivity in intricate electrocatalytic nitrogen transformations.
10.1021_acsami.6c10462: Aqueous zinc-nickel batteries show great potential for large-scale energy storage because of their inherent safety, high working voltage, and high theoretical specific capacity. However, zinc dendrites and hydrogen evolution side reactions lead to poor stability of zinc electrodes, resulting in a short cycle life of zinc-nickel batteries. To mitigate these challenges, an In-anchored zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 (In-ZIF8) interface layer is constructed in-situ on ZnO as an anode active material of zinc-nickel batteries. The ZIF8 layer with high zinc affinity and a porous structure promotes the dissociation of Zn(OH)42- ions and ion migration, contributing to uniform ion distribution. The anchored In serves as an electron conductor to uniformize the electric field. Meanwhile, the in-situ formation of the interface creates a competing coordination environment, leading to charge redistribution at the ZnO-protective layer interface and causing the reconfigured electronic structure and reduced band gap, further homogenizing the electric field and facilitating the reaction kinetics. With synergistic regulation of mass and charge transfer, dendrite-free and side reaction-free Zn deposition is achieved. A symmetric cell with the In-ZIF8-modified zinc electrode exhibits good cycling stability (over 500 h at 17 mA cm-2, 17 mAh cm-2). The assembled zinc-nickel battery (N/P = 1) delivers an extended cycling lifetime, achieving a stable cycling performance over 840 h for the 5 Ah battery configuration at 10 A (∼138 mA cm-2). This work proposes a facile method of reasonable interface engineering for improving the stability of the zinc electrode at high current density.
10.1021_acsnano.5c09592: Airborne pathogens and pollution control typically necessitate multiple membranes, each specializing in efficient aerosol filtration, moisture regulation, or antimicrobial protection. Integrating all these functions into a single membrane is highly advantageous but remains inherently challenging due to material incompatibility and inevitable performance trade-offs. Here, we present a photoactive Janus nanofibrous membrane for highly efficient air purification, engineered via sequential electrospinning. This asymmetric membrane features a biomimetic cactus spine and pollen structures formed within a hydrophilic biopolymer matrix with the embedding of nitrogen-doped carbon quantum dots (N-CQDs) on one side and hydrophobic microchannels on the other, together creating interfacial chemical gradients that drive unidirectional water transport. The nanofibrous membranes exhibit simultaneous size-exclusion sieving and electrostatic capture through quantum-confined charge polarization, achieving over 99.59% retention of PM 0.3 aerosols. Under UV activation, the N-CQDs generate tunable reactive oxygen species, enabling contact-free pathogen inactivation, which is further enhanced by water-mediated destabilization of microbial cell membranes, resulting in a 6-log (99.9999%) reduction of both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria within 30 min. The membranes demonstrate exceptional operational durability, retaining 98.5% filtration efficiency after 10 working cycles, outperforming conventional membranes susceptible to water moisture-induced degradation. This work presents a versatile platform for advanced multifunctional air purification membranes, enabling a wide range of applications spanning biomedical isolation gowns, smart ventilation systems, and reusable respiratory devices.
10.1021_jacs.6c02109: The rational design of electrocatalysts has long relied on thermodynamic descriptors based on intermediate binding energies. However, such descriptors often overlook potential-dependent surface charging inherent to electrolysis, limiting its ability to capture the reaction kinetics under operational conditions. Here, we identify the potential of zero charge (PZC), which regulates the interfacial electron energy landscape, as a kinetic descriptor for CO 2 electroreduction. By evaluating 11 catalysts across a wide pH range (acidic to alkaline), we reveal strong correlations between overpotential and PZC for multiple reaction pathways, including CO, formate, and multicarbon products. Through integrated electrochemical analysis, isotope labeling, in situ spectroscopy, and computational modeling, we show that PZC fundamentally regulates electron-transfer kinetics. At a given negetive potential, a catalyst with a more positive PZC introduces a larger electrostatic contribution to the electron energy to offset their lower chemical potential, which accelerates electron transfer to both the catalyst surface and reaction intermediates. This PZC-based kinetic descriptor further extends to the acidic hydrogen evolution reaction, highlighting its broad applicability across electrocatalytic systems.
10.1039_d4gc06334a: Using OSN, a homogeneous Pd catalyst in AZD4625 synthesis is separated and reused for five cycles, maintaining over 90% conversion.
10.26599_nr.2026.94908760: Strengthening the stability of metal–oxygen (M–O) bonds in catalysts is imperative for the advancement of efficient and durable electrocatalytic water splitting. Herein, using a mild boron-reduction strategy, a self-supported electrode with robust Co–B bonds was constructed. The Co–B@Co(OH)2–Ru/nickel foam (NF) (Co–B@CRN) electrode demonstrates low overpotentials for alkaline hydrogen evolution reaction (HER, 20 mV) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER, 160 mV) at 10 mA·cm−2. Furthermore, long-term stability was achieved for over 400 h at 10 mA·cm−2 and 270 h at 200 mA·cm−2, respectively. For overall water splitting, the assembled electrolyzer exhibited a low voltage of 1.40 V at 10 mA·cm−2, with stable operation maintained for over 240 h. Detailed extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) characterization verified the mixed valence state of Co and the Co–B coordination environment. Further electronic analysis indicated strong hybridization between Co d-orbitals and B p-orbitals. The B bonding induced a downward shift in the d-band center at the Co site, thereby significantly suppressing metal leaching during catalysis and stabilizing electronic structure regulation. This research shows that the boron reduction strategy offers an effective dynamic regulation mechanism for the electronic structures and coordination environments of transition metals, enabling a highly efficient and stable overall water splitting process.
